title: The Distribution of School Spending Impacts
research_question: How much does an increase in public K–12 per-pupil school spending causally affect student outcomes such as test scores, high school graduation, and college-going? How do these marginal effects vary across spending types (capital versus non-capital), student economic backgrounds, baseline spending levels, and geographic settings, and what range of impacts can be expected from future spending policies in new contexts?
data_description: The authors compile a dataset of 31 studies published or made public between 1995 and December 2020 that estimate the impact of policy-induced changes in K–12 public school spending on student outcomes in the United States. Studies were located through prior literature reviews, Google Scholar searches, citation tracing, and an open call to active researchers. For each study, the authors extract or compute a common parameter: the effect of a $1,000 per-pupil increase in school spending (in 2018 CPI-adjusted dollars), sustained over four years, on standardized student outcomes. Outcomes captured include test scores/proficiency rates (24 studies), educational attainment such as high school graduation, dropout, and college enrollment (12 studies), and longer-run outcomes like wages and income mobility (3 studies). For each study, they also record the policy-induced change in per-pupil spending, standard errors, sample populations, geography, and spending type (capital vs. non-capital).
institutional_context: Public K–12 education is one of the largest components of U.S. government spending, and ongoing state Supreme Court cases and policy debates hinge on whether and how much increased school funding improves student outcomes. Over the past several decades, U.S. states and districts have implemented a wide variety of policies that altered school spending, including state school finance reforms, local capital bond referenda, Title I funding rules, school improvement grants, and funding formula changes triggered by enrollment shifts or recessions. These policies vary in size, target populations (e.g., low-income districts, rural schools, large urban districts), and whether funds support operational expenditures (teachers, materials) or long-lived capital projects (buildings, renovations). The diversity of policies across states, time periods, and contexts—combined with differences in baseline spending, urbanicity, and student demographics—creates substantial heterogeneity in how spending changes translate into classroom inputs and student outcomes.
